title: In many ways, nothing has really surpassed King Kong (2005) in the epic adventure genre

commenti.body:
I actually feel like "epic adventure" kind of devalues it.

I always find the label "adventure" to be a little problematic because it entails a kind of quixotic spirit to the film, and while some films certainly fit that label, Sir Peter Jackson's King Kong is not one of them. The island is the most menacing and nightmarish that its ever been in any King Kong film, and the ending tremendously downbeat. In that sense, it has more in common with Chinatown than with Raiders of the Lost Ark.

Honestly I find it a bit of a drag, which is a death sentence for a genre that lives or dies on being exciting and fun.  
  
The Mummy, The Man Who Would Be King, multiple adaptations of The Lost World, Romancing the Stone, heck even Kong: Skull Island do the genre miles better in my eyes. Flow and moment-to-moment enjoyment (generally via fun, atmosphere, or awe) are so key and are where Peter Jackson's film massively drop the ball time and time again.

Most of the critisism regarding the movie have been geared toward it's running time. I'm one of those weird people who absolutely loved the entirety of it, and for one, glad that Peter Jackson wasn't willing to cut things down. Too many adventure movies tend to jump straight into the action part as soon as it begins after spending fifteen or so minutes of dumping information after information on the audience regarding who the characters are, what they are doing etc etc. I don't want to hear "as you already know..." or listen to characters reminding the other who they are and why they are here every time they talk. I want to *see* the context, I want to see how they got into the situation in the first place. To throw it all at us at once simply makes the story feels less grand in scale, even if the story happens in a bigger world. 

King Kong does that part very well. It takes it's ample time setting up the story and characters before setting off. There are many instances of mundanity throughout the movie that has been unfairly called useless filler material, even when all of them serves a purpose in either setting up the richness of the world they are in or building the character's relationship, including Anne and Kong's. As a result, the movie feels complete, even more complete in a sense than many other action adventure movies I've seen throughout the years. I don't think a remake could have been more faithful in adapting the grandeur of the original film.

Your comments are making me want to revisit the movie, which I haven't seen in a very long time.

I love the original and think that in its best scenes it achieves a truly dreamlike/nightmarish quality.
